title: Dow Rises, Tech Stocks Surge; S&P 500, Nasdaq Rally as Oil Falls, Yields Climb
body:
U.S. equities opened on a positive note on Monday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbing 0.6% and both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite rallying roughly 0.8% after a volatile week. The bounce was anchored by a resurgence in technology shares, while energy stocks slipped as crude oil fell back toward $85 a barrel. Meanwhile, Treasury yields nudged higher, reflecting a modest shift in investor sentiment toward risk‑on positioning.

The Dow’s advance was led by a mix of industrial and consumer‑goods names that posted solid earnings beats, notably Caterpillar, which rose 2.1% after reporting better‑than‑expected sales in its construction equipment segment. The S&P 500’s gains were broader, with the information technology sector posting the largest percentage increase of any group. Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia each added between 1.5% and 2.3%, lifting the Nasdaq’s tech‑heavy index to its highest level in three weeks. Analysts attribute the rebound to a combination of easing concerns over chip‑related supply constraints and a renewed optimism about the rollout of artificial‑intelligence applications across enterprise software.

Energy stocks, by contrast, were the day’s laggards. Brent crude slipped 1.2% to $84.90 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate settled at $81.45, down 1.4% from the previous close. The decline came after the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported a larger‑than‑expected build in crude inventories, suggesting that demand growth may be tempering amid lingering inflationary pressures. As a result, the energy‑focused S&P 500 Energy Index fell 0.9%, dragging down some of the broader market’s momentum.

Bond markets moved in tandem with equities, with the benchmark 10‑year Treasury yield edging up to 4.45%, its highest level in six months. The modest rise in yields reflects a subtle recalibration of expectations for the Federal Reserve’s policy path. While the central bank has signaled that it will maintain its current stance for now, investors are beginning to price in the possibility of another rate hike later in the year if inflation fails to stay below the 2% target. Higher yields typically make fixed‑income assets more attractive relative to stocks, but the current spread between Treasury yields and corporate credit remains wide enough to keep risk‑appetites intact.

The market’s overall tone was shaped by a mix of macroeconomic data and corporate earnings. A fresh batch of consumer‑price figures released on Friday showed inflation cooling slightly, with the core CPI rising 0.2% month‑over‑month, well under the 0.5% median forecast. This modest deceleration has eased some of the pressure on the Fed’s tightening cycle, allowing investors to re‑enter growth‑oriented stocks that had been penalized earlier in the week. At the same time, the latest batch of earnings reports—particularly from the technology sector—demonstrated that many firms are successfully navigating supply‑chain disruptions and are capitalizing on heightened demand for cloud and AI services.

Looking ahead, market participants will be watching several key events that could steer the next trading session. The Federal Reserve’s policy meeting scheduled for next week remains a focal point; any hint of a shift in the rate‑hike timetable could quickly reshape the risk‑on/risk‑off balance. Additionally, the upcoming release of the U.S. jobs report on Friday will provide further insight into the health of the labor market and its impact on consumer spending. Finally, oil prices will continue to be a wildcard, as geopolitical developments in the Middle East and inventory data could reignite volatility in the energy sector. For now, the blend of tech‑driven optimism and cautious optimism about inflation suggests that U.S. equities may maintain their upward trajectory, provided that macro‑economic surprises remain limited.
